title: Making Scripts Executable ⚙️
description: Turn your script into an executable program with chmod and run it from anywhere.

slides.title: Permissions Matter 🔐
slides.content:
## Can't Run? No Execute Permission!

Linux/macOS have permissions: read (r), write (w), execute (x).
By default, a new text file is not executable. You need to give it the execute permission.

Use `ls -l` to see permissions.

Example: `-rw-r--r--` → no `x`.

slides.title: Grant Execute with chmod ✅
slides.content: `chmod +x script.sh` adds execute permission for everyone.

quizData.question: What does `chmod +x myscript.sh` do?
quizData.explanation: `chmod +x` adds the execute permission, allowing you to run the script directly.

slides.title: Running the Executable 🚀
slides.content:
## Direct Execution
Once it's executable, run it with:
```
./hello.sh
```
The `./` means "in the current directory". Without it, the shell looks in system `PATH` folders.

quizData.question: You can run an executable script without `./` if it's in the current directory.
quizData.explanation: You need `./` to tell the shell that the script is in the current directory, unless the directory is in the PATH.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Add to PATH
If you place your script in a folder that's in your `PATH` (like `/usr/local/bin`), you can run it from anywhere without `./`.
